0.title: 3 John: Walking in Truth, Tested by Character
0.overview:
The message. Third John tells a faithful Christian to keep his door open to those who carry the gospel, and shows by contrast what happens when a church leader closes it. The elder praises Gaius for walking in the truth and caring for travelling missionaries, “strangers as they are” (v. 5); he exposes Diotrephes, who “likes to put himself first” (v. 9); and he commends Demetrius as a man to trust. Its counsel fits in one line: “do not imitate evil but imitate good” (v. 11). It is the shortest book in the Bible, fifteen verses and about 219 words in the Greek, and one of the most personal: a private note to one man, warm, direct and full of the texture of real church life. It never quotes the Old Testament and offers no formal doctrinal argument, yet it sets two men side by side in a way no reader forgets.

Background: the writer. The author is again “the elder” (v. 1), the man who wrote 2 John, a title that speaks both of age and of recognised standing among the churches (see elders). The church from early times identified him as John the son of Zebedee, the apostle who wrote the Gospel and 1 John, by tradition the last of the Twelve still living, who had known Jesus in the flesh. Some scholars think of a different John, a teacher known as John the Elder, or a circle of the apostle’s disciples; but the language and concerns of the three letters (truth, love, witness, walking in the truth) point to one mind, and this commentary holds that the elder is the apostle. The same tradition places him in old age at Ephesus, in the Roman province of Asia, so the letter was probably written there, about AD 85–95, close in time to 1 and 2 John. The elder still claims authority over churches he cannot visit at once, and he means to come (vv. 10, 14).

The first readers. The letter is addressed “to the beloved Gaius, whom I love in truth” (v. 1). Gaius was one of the commonest names in the Roman world, and nothing links this man with the Gaius of Corinth, Macedonia or Derbe. He was probably a believer of means in a church near the elder, perhaps one of his own converts (“my children”, v. 4). The elder prays for his health and for all to go well with him, “as it goes well with your soul” (v. 2), and loves him dearly without embarrassment.

Missionaries on the road. The churches of Asia met in homes, and the gospel spread through preachers who moved between them on foot along the Roman roads. Inns had a bad name, so travellers depended on believers for a bed, a meal and supplies for the next stage. These brothers had “gone out for the sake of the name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles” (v. 7): they would not take money from unbelievers, unlike the wandering teachers of philosophy and religion who lived by their audiences. So the churches were to “send them on their journey in a manner worthy of God” (v. 6). Christian hospitality was famous, and in 2 John the elder had warned against giving it to false teachers. Here he commends giving it generously to faithful ones. The two letters are mirror images: together they show how hospitality, authority and truth belong together.

What prompted the letter. The elder had “written something to the church” (v. 9), perhaps a letter commending these missionaries; some think it was 2 John, though that cannot be shown. But Diotrephes, a leader in that church, would not acknowledge the elder’s authority. He was “talking wicked nonsense” against him, refused to welcome the brothers, stopped those who wanted to, and put them out of the church (v. 10). He is not accused of false teaching. He is something perhaps more common: a man who really held office in the church but treated its authority as his own, and used the church’s structures to keep himself first. The elder names him plainly, without bitterness, and turns to Gaius, whose home may now have been the missionaries’ only open door. Demetrius, who has “received a good testimony from everyone, and from the truth itself” (v. 12), probably carried this short letter, a single sheet of papyrus, and came with the elder’s word to receive him.

How the letter makes its case. It moves through three men. Verses 1–4 are the greeting and the elder’s joy at Gaius’s faithfulness: “I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth” (v. 4). Verses 5–8 praise his care for the missionaries and give the principle behind it: “we ought to support people like these, that we may be fellow workers for the truth” (v. 8). Verses 9–10 expose Diotrephes and promise to deal with him in person. Verses 11–12 give the lesson, imitate good, not evil, and commend Demetrius as the good example. Verses 13–15 close, as 2 John does, with the hope that “we will talk face to face” (v. 14), and ask Gaius to “greet the friends, each by name” (v. 15).

Where it leads: to Christ. Jesus is not named in the letter, yet he is its centre. The missionaries went out “for the sake of the name” (v. 7), the name for which the apostles rejoiced to suffer dishonour (Acts 5:41). Jesus himself said of those he sent, “Whoever receives you receives me” (Matthew 10:40), so to welcome his messengers is to welcome him, and to shut them out is to shut him out. The truth in which Gaius walks is finally Christ, “the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). And Diotrephes is the exact opposite of the Lord who taught that “whoever would be first among you must be slave of all” (Mark 10:44), for “even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve” (Mark 10:45). Those who do good show that they are from God; whoever does evil “has not seen God” (v. 11).

For us. Third John asks believers to open their homes and their purses to those who carry the gospel, and to count it a share in the work: anyone can be a fellow worker for the truth. It warns church leaders, and every member, against the love of being first, which can sit comfortably beside sound doctrine and still do great harm. It reminds us that a good name among God’s people, and before the truth itself, is worth having. And it shows that the church is a fellowship of people known and greeted by name.

1.title: Truth, Hospitality, and the Test of Character
1.overview:
Where we are. Third John has only one chapter, so this is the whole letter: a private note from the elder to his friend Gaius. Where 2 John told a church to shut its door to teachers who deny Christ, its companion tells one man to keep his door open to those who carry Christ’s name.

The message. The truth shows itself in how we treat Christ’s servants. To walk in the truth is to open your home and your purse to those who have gone out for the sake of the name, and so to become their fellow worker. The love of being first does the opposite, whatever its creed: it shuts out the brothers and drives out anyone who disagrees. So the elder sets three men before Gaius and asks him whom he will copy: “do not imitate evil but imitate good” (v. 11).

Why it was said. Travelling missionaries depended on the churches for a bed, a meal and supplies, and in one church Diotrephes had refused them and put out those who welcomed them (see the introduction). Gaius’s home may now have been their only open door, and he needed courage to keep it open.

How the chapter makes its case. The greeting prays that Gaius’s body will do as well as his soul (vv. 1–2), and the elder rejoices that his children walk in the truth (vv. 3–4). That walk looks like faithful care for strangers who went out for the name, care that makes the host a partner in their work (vv. 5–8). Diotrephes is the dark contrast: slander, a shut door and discipline turned into a weapon (vv. 9–10). The lesson follows, imitate good, with Demetrius as the example (vv. 11–12). The letter closes with peace and greetings, each by name (vv. 13–15).

Where it leads. Christ is never named, yet everything turns on him. The missionaries carried his name, and he had said, “Whoever receives you receives me” (Matthew 10:40). The truth Gaius walks in is the one who is the truth (John 14:6). And the man who must be first stands opposite the Lord who, though first of all, “came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). To have seen God is to have seen that Son, and to begin to look like him.

For us. Open your home and your giving to faithful gospel workers, and count it a share in their work. Look for the love of being first in yourself before you look for it in others, and aim to be a believer of whom the truth itself can speak well.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A healthy soul is the measure of a life that is going well. The elder writes to one man he loves “in truth”, with a love grounded in the gospel they share (v. 1), and prays that Gaius’s health and affairs will go as well as his soul already does (v. 2): a striking compliment, and a quiet ordering of what matters most.
verseByVerse.theology:
Love in Truth

On love in truth and the prayer for body and soul, see the note on vv. 1–2.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Gaius’s soul was healthy enough to be the measure of the prayer.

Now: Pray for the whole person, knowing the soul matters most.

verseByVerse.quote: The elder to the beloved Gaius, whom I love in truth. Beloved, I pray that all may go well with you and that you may be in good health, as it goes well with your soul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The elder greets a friend he loves because of the truth they share, and prays that his body and affairs will do as well as his soul already does.

The elder to the beloved Gaius. The writer is the same elder as in 2 John, the apostle in old age (see the introduction). Gaius was a very common name (compare Romans 16:23; 1 Corinthians 1:14), and this one cannot be identified: a faithful member, perhaps a leader, of a church in the elder’s care, possibly one of his converts (v. 4). “Beloved” comes four times in this short letter; the old apostle cannot stop calling his friend dear.

Whom I love in truth. Sincere love, grounded in the gospel they share (2 John 1).

That all may go well with you and that you may be in good health. “Go well” (euodousthai) pictures a good road, though in ordinary use it meant simply to do well. Such wishes were common in ancient letters; perhaps Gaius had been unwell. The apostle of eternal life also prays for his friend’s body: God made bodies, and his servants care about them.

As it goes well with your soul. John prays that the rest of Gaius’s life would prosper as his soul already does: the soul sets the standard. A searching measure: how would your body look if it were as healthy as your soul?

Where a healthy soul comes from. No soul is born healthy. “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick,” Jesus said; “I came not to call the righteous, but sinners” (Mark 2:17). Gaius’s soul was going well because it had been healed, at great cost: “By his wounds you have been healed” (1 Peter 2:24). Christ had opened the good road his soul was on. Bodies weaken and fortunes rise and fall, but a soul made whole by the Saviour is already on the road to the resurrection, where body and soul will be well together.

Is it unspiritual to pray for health and ordinary needs? No. Jesus taught us to ask for daily bread (Matthew 6:11), and Paul rejoiced that God had mercy on the sick Epaphroditus (Philippians 2:27). Praying for a friend’s health, job, journey or exams is an act of love. The danger lies in getting the order wrong: praying earnestly for the body and never for the soul, or treating God as a supplier of comforts rather than a Father to be known. Ask for health and for holiness, and trust him with the answer.

Where Christians differ: does this verse promise health and wealth to believers? The prosperity gospel uses it to teach that God wants every believer healthy and rich, and that faith secures it. This commentary’s view: this is a conventional greeting and a personal prayer for a friend, not a promise to all believers. John prays for Gaius’s health; he does not guarantee it. Scripture shows godly believers who were sick (2 Timothy 4:20; Philippians 2:25–27) and poor (James 2:5), and teaches contentment (1 Timothy 6:6–10). It is right to pray for one another’s welfare, but to read this verse as a promise of prosperity turns a greeting into a guarantee God never gave.
verseByVerse.note: By word count in Greek, the shortest book of the Bible. Gaius was a common name; this one is otherwise unknown.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The truth is seen when it is lived. The travelling brothers knew Gaius walked in the truth because they had stayed in his house and felt it (v. 3), and nothing gives the old elder more joy than to hear that his spiritual children are living that way (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology:
No Greater Joy

A shepherd’s greatest joy is not his own experience but his children’s faithfulness (see the note on vv. 3–4).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Gaius’s faithfulness was known by what others experienced of it.

Now: A life that walks in truth leaves traces others can see.

verseByVerse.quote: For I rejoiced greatly when the brothers came and testified to your truth, as indeed you are walking in the truth. I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing gives the elder greater joy than to hear that his spiritual children, Gaius among them, are living out the truth.

The brothers came and testified to your truth. “The brothers” are travelling missionaries who had stayed with Gaius and reported back, probably the men of verses 5–8. “Your truth” is the truth as Gaius lived it, visible enough for strangers to vouch for.

No greater joy. “Greater” is a doubled form in Greek, for emphasis. “My children” are spiritual children, those he led to Christ or pastored. A Christian leader’s or parent’s greatest joy is to see those in their care living faithfully (1 Thessalonians 2:19–20).

What an old man counts as his greatest joy. He had been called from his father’s boat by the Son of God. He had seen water become wine, the dead raised, the Lord transfigured. He had stood at the cross, run to the empty tomb, and eaten fish with the risen Christ on the beach. Yet his greatest joy is not his experiences but his children’s faithfulness: the heart of a true shepherd.

The joy John learned from Jesus. On the night before the cross he had heard Jesus pray, “I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world … and they have kept your word” (John 17:6). The Lord spoke of keeping them and losing none (17:12), and asked “that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves” (17:13). John’s joy is a share in Christ’s own joy over his people, the joy for which he endured the cross: a people walking in his truth. He will have them, every one.

I have no spiritual children. Does this joy apply to me? Most believers have more than they realise: a Sunday school class, the younger believer you encouraged, the colleague who first heard of Christ from you, your own sons and daughters. If you have none yet, pray for some, and look for one person to invest in. And whenever you hear that any believer is walking in the truth, you may share the elder’s gladness. It is a family joy, for everyone who loves the family.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: To care for those who carry the gospel is to share in their work. Gaius welcomed brothers he had never met, and is asked to send them on as God would (vv. 5–6), because they went out for Christ’s name and took nothing from unbelievers (v. 7). So supporting them is a duty and a partnership: those who give become “fellow workers for the truth” (v. 8). This is the other side of 2 John 10–11, where the door is shut to false teachers.
verseByVerse.theology:
Fellow Workers for the Truth

On hosts as fellow workers, and on this as the counterpart of 2 John, see the note on vv. 5–8.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The missionaries took nothing from the Gentiles and relied on the churches.

Now: Those who support gospel workers share their work.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, it is a faithful thing you do in all your efforts for these brothers, strangers as they are, who testified to your love before the church. You will do well to send them on their journey in a manner worthy of God. For they have gone out for the sake of the name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles. Therefore we ought to support people like these, that we may be fellow workers for the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Caring for those who carry the gospel is faithfulness to Christ, and it makes the giver a partner in their work. Gaius did it for strangers, and the elder asks him to keep doing it.

It is a faithful thing you do. Gaius’s spare room, table and purse were acts of faithfulness to Christ: this is what walking in the truth (vv. 3–4) looked like for him, and it prepares the contrast with Diotrephes (v. 10). With 2 John it makes one teaching: close the door to those who deny Christ (2 John 10), and open it wide to those who carry his name.

Strangers as they are. Gaius did not know them personally (Romans 12:13; Hebrews 13:2). The New Testament word for hospitality, philoxenia, means love of strangers: not entertaining friends, but opening the door to people you do not know because they belong to Christ.

Before the church. The missionaries told the elder’s church; now kindness done in a private house is read of in churches everywhere.

Send them on their journey in a manner worthy of God. “Send on” (propempsas) was the regular word for supplying missionaries for the next stage of the road (Romans 15:24; Titus 3:13). “Worthy of God” means as God himself would treat his servants: not what is comfortable or customary, but what befits those who represent the God who gave his Son.

Accepting nothing from the Gentiles. They took no money from pagans, so that no one could say they preached for profit (2 Corinthians 11:7–9; 1 Thessalonians 2:9). Travelling philosophers begged from their audiences; these men refused, and so depended on Christians.

For the sake of the name. Christ’s name (Acts 5:41), given him when he had humbled himself to death on a cross, the name at which every knee will bow (Philippians 2:9–10); these men had left home to carry it to people who had never heard it. Jesus said, “Whoever receives you receives me” (Matthew 10:40). To house such men was to side openly with that name, and in receiving them Gaius received the Lord himself. One day the King will say to every faithful host, “I was a stranger and you welcomed me” (Matthew 25:35).

We ought to support people like these. “Support” means hold up from underneath: a duty owed by people who were themselves reached because someone once went out for the name.

Fellow workers for the truth. Those who support gospel workers share in their work and its fruit (Philippians 1:5; 4:14–17). The woman who gave a bed to a missionary in the first century has a share in every church he planted.

In everyday life. Somewhere tonight a missionary your church supports is unpacking in a rented flat far from home. The gift, the prayer by name, the email asking for news: each is the work Gaius did with his spare room, and an echo of the welcome Christ has prepared in his Father’s house (John 14:2).

How do I know which missionaries and ministries to support? Ask the questions this letter and 2 John raise. Are they faithful to the teaching of Christ? Have they gone out for his name, or their own? Are they sent by a faithful church and accountable to it, rather than self-appointed? Are they honest with money? Start with workers your own church has sent, and get to know them. Give regularly rather than only when moved by an appeal, and generously, in a manner worthy of God.

Must I host strangers in my home? What about safety? Hospitality is commanded of all believers (Romans 12:13; 1 Peter 4:9), but its form varies. In John’s day it meant travelling Christians known through the churches, often carrying letters of commendation, as Demetrius probably did (v. 12). Wisdom is not unbelief: host people your church vouches for, think about the safety of children and vulnerable people in your home, and where a bed would be unwise, offer a meal, a lift or a gift. The heart of it is an open hand towards Christ’s servants.
verseByVerse.note: Travelling missionaries relied on believers for food and lodging rather than taking money from pagans.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Conduct, not position, shows who has truly seen God. Diotrephes holds office, but everything he does, rejecting the elder, slandering him, turning the brothers away and putting out those who welcome them, grows from one root: he likes to put himself first (vv. 9–10). So Gaius must imitate good, not evil, for doing good marks those who are from God (v. 11), and Demetrius, commended by everyone, by the truth and by the elder, shows him what good looks like (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology:
Diotrephes and Demetrius

On Diotrephes, see vv. 9–10; on whom to imitate, see vv. 11–12.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Demetrius had a good testimony from everyone and from the truth itself.

Now: The love of being first shows itself in whom it shuts out.

verseByVerse.quote: I have written something to the church, but Diotrephes, who likes to put himself first, does not acknowledge our authority. So if I come, I will bring up what he is doing, talking wicked nonsense against us. And not content with that, he refuses to welcome the brothers, and also stops those who want to and puts them out of the church.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A leader who loves first place shuts out anyone who threatens it, and the elder will not let it pass. He promises to bring into the open all that Diotrephes is doing.

I have written something to the church. Diotrephes ignored or suppressed it (on what it was, see “Uncertain wording” below).

Diotrephes, who likes to put himself first. His name means nourished by Zeus; otherwise unknown, he was apparently a leader in the church. The word (philoprōteuōn) occurs only here; John may have coined it. His problem was not false doctrine but pride, which turns every relationship into a contest for first place. Underneath, the love of first place is often fear: the man who must be first is afraid of being nothing. Only the gospel cures that fear at the root, because it gives a sinner a worth he did not win and cannot lose, as a child loved by God (1 John 3:1). The elders Peter describes are the opposite, “not domineering over those in your charge” (1 Peter 5:3).

Does not acknowledge our authority. Literally does not receive us. The same verb appears in verse 10, where he “refuses to welcome the brothers”: refusing the elder and refusing his messengers are one act.

If I come, I will bring up what he is doing. “Bring up” (hypomnēsō) means call attention to: John will deal with him in the open.

Talking wicked nonsense against us. Frothy, baseless talk (phlyarōn), and malicious: he was slandering the apostle.

He refuses to welcome the brothers, and puts them out of the church. He turned the missionaries away, perhaps because they came from John, and expelled those who welcomed them: church discipline abused for personal power.

The disciple who once wanted the first seat. Long before, John and his brother James had asked Jesus for the seats at his right and left in glory (Mark 10:35–41). Jesus told them that “whoever would be first among you must be slave of all. For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:44–45). John watched Jesus take the last place at the cross, and learned the lesson slowly. He knew Diotrephes from the inside: he had once wanted the same seat.

In everyday life. Where do you love to be first? The signs are small: needing the last word, resenting another’s praise, finding correction hard. Pick one this week and do the opposite, as one who already has, in Christ, a place no one can take.

How should a church respond to a controlling leader like Diotrephes? John names the marks: love of first place, rejection of accountability, slander, refusing fellowship to faithful believers, expelling those who disagree. He does not ignore it. A church facing such a leader should appeal to other elders, insist on accountability according to Scripture (1 Timothy 5:19–20), and protect those he wrongs. Putting faithful people out is an abuse of discipline, which is for unrepentant sin, carried out by the church through a careful process (Matthew 18:15–17; 1 Corinthians 5), not for those who will not submit to one man’s control.

Is naming Diotrephes in a letter not just gossip? No. Gossip talks about someone behind his back to harm him. John names a public wrong done by a public leader, to a responsible believer, and promises to confront him face to face. Some wrongs, especially the abuse of power, must be named, or the vulnerable go unprotected. Yet John shows restraint: he says what Diotrephes is doing without guessing at hidden motives, and asks Gaius to start no campaign; he will deal with it himself.

Uncertain wording. “I have written something to the church” does not say what. It may be a letter now lost, perhaps one commending the missionaries; some think it is 2 John, though that cannot be shown. What is clear is that the elder had written, and that Diotrephes would not receive it.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, do not imitate evil but imitate good. Whoever does good is from God; whoever does evil has not seen God. Demetrius has received a good testimony from everyone, and from the truth itself. We also add our testimony, and you know that our testimony is true.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Copy what is good, not what is evil, because a person’s conduct shows whether he truly knows God. Demetrius is the good example.

Do not imitate evil but imitate good. With Diotrephes and Demetrius before him, Gaius must choose whom to copy (1 Corinthians 11:1), and character is formed by that choice.

Whoever does evil has not seen God. The tests of 1 John in brief (1 John 3:6, 10). Conduct reveals a person’s relationship with God; it does not purchase it, for no child of God does good perfectly, and the one life that did, Christ’s, is counted as theirs. Diotrephes held office, yet his behaviour raised the question whether he had ever seen God.

Demetrius has received a good testimony from everyone. Probably the bearer of this letter, commended so that Gaius will welcome him.

And from the truth itself. His life so matched the gospel that the truth spoke for him, as a key that turns a lock testifies that it was cut for it (see “Uncertain wording” below).

You know that our testimony is true. Three witnesses speak for Demetrius, and the last is the elder, staking his apostolic authority on a man we would never otherwise have heard of.

Seen in the face of Christ. What does John mean by seeing God, when “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:18)? He means knowing God as he has shown himself in his Son: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). To have seen God is to have looked at Christ by faith and been changed, for “we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image” (2 Corinthians 3:18). That is why doing good is the evidence: people come to resemble the one they gaze at. Diotrephes’ love of first place showed that he had never truly looked at the one who took the last.

Does “whoever does evil has not seen God” mean that a Christian who sins is not saved? No. As in his first letter (1 John 3:6, 9), John means the pattern of a life, not single sins; he also says, “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1 John 1:8). A believer who struggles with sin and runs to Christ is not the one John describes.

Whom should I imitate if my own church leaders disappoint me? First Christ, the only perfect example (1 Peter 2:21). Then look for the Demetriuses: believers, perhaps not leaders at all, whose lives match the truth; and for faithful Christians of the past, whose lives were tested to the end (Hebrews 13:7). Do not let a Diotrephes drive you from the church; one proud leader is not the whole body. Pray for your leaders, honour what is good in them, and speak to them humbly about what is not.

Uncertain wording. John does not explain how the truth itself testified to Demetrius. Most take it that his life matched the gospel so closely that the truth spoke for him; others think of Christ, who is the truth (John 14:6), or of the Spirit, whom John calls the truth (1 John 5:6). The first is likely, though for John the truth is never far from the person of Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Some things can only be said face to face. As in 2 John, the letter breaks off with the hope of a visit (vv. 13–14), and closes with peace for Gaius and greetings to the friends “each by name” (v. 15): a church of people known personally, as their Shepherd knows them.
verseByVerse.theology:
Face to Face, and Peace

On peace and greeting each by name, see the note on vv. 13–15.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: 2 and 3 John read as companion letters on hospitality.

Now: The church is a fellowship of friends known by name.

verseByVerse.quote: I had much to write to you, but I would rather not write with pen and ink. I hope to see you soon, and we will talk face to face. Peace be to you. The friends greet you. Greet the friends, each by name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The elder would rather say the rest in person, and he closes with peace for Gaius and a greeting for every friend, by name.

Pen and ink. A reed pen on a single sheet of papyrus, as in 2 John 12 (see letters and scrolls).

Face to face. Literally mouth to mouth, again: the elder wants to sit with his friend.

Peace be to you. The Hebrew greeting shalom, and the risen Christ’s greeting (John 20:19), spoken into a church troubled by Diotrephes. “You” is singular: a father’s word to a faithful son at the end of a hard conversation.

Greet the friends, each by name. “Friends” echoes Jesus, who called his disciples friends (John 15:13–15), and the Good Shepherd “calls his own sheep by name” (John 10:3). The elder who has named Gaius, Diotrephes and Demetrius closes by asking Gaius to greet everyone by name: a small picture of the Shepherd, who knows every one of his sheep and loses none in the crowd. When he comes, he will greet each of his own by name, and we will see him face to face.

How can I have peace in a church torn by conflict? Peace begins with Christ, who is our peace (Ephesians 2:14), not with the conflict being settled. Then refuse to feed the conflict: no gossip, no taking sides on personalities, and prayer for everyone involved, including those who have wronged you. Do what is right where you are responsible, as Gaius kept welcoming the brothers; support faithful leaders who are dealing with it; be a Demetrius. And remember that the church belongs to Christ, who will put things right in his time.

1.text: <sup>1</sup>The elder to the beloved Gaius, whom I love in truth.<sup>2</sup>Beloved, I pray that all may go well with you and that you may be in good health, as it goes well with your soul.<sup>3</sup>For I rejoiced greatly when the brothers came and testified to your truth, as indeed you are walking in the truth.<sup>4</sup>I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth.<sup>5</sup>Beloved, it is a faithful thing you do in all your efforts for these brothers, strangers as they are,<sup>6</sup>who testified to your love before the church. You will do well to send them on their journey in a manner worthy of God.<sup>7</sup>For they have gone out for the sake of the name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles.<sup>8</sup>Therefore we ought to support people like these, that we may be fellow workers for the truth.<sup>9</sup>I have written something to the church, but Diotrephes, who likes to put himself first, does not acknowledge our authority.<sup>10</sup>So if I come, I will bring up what he is doing, talking wicked nonsense against us. And not content with that, he refuses to welcome the brothers, and also stops those who want to and puts them out of the church.<sup>11</sup>Beloved, do not imitate evil but imitate good. Whoever does good is from God; whoever does evil has not seen God.<sup>12</sup>Demetrius has received a good testimony from everyone, and from the truth itself. We also add our testimony, and you know that our testimony is true.<sup>13</sup>I had much to write to you, but I would rather not write with pen and ink.<sup>14</sup>I hope to see you soon, and we will talk face to face.<sup>15</sup>Peace be to you. The friends greet you. Greet the friends, each by name.

keyVerse.quote: Beloved, do not imitate evil but imitate good. Whoever does good is from God; whoever does evil has not seen God.
keyVerse.note: This verse gathers the letter into one choice. Gaius has two men in front of him, Diotrephes and Demetrius, and the elder tells him which to follow and why: what a person does shows whether he has truly seen God. We become like those we copy, and the good worth copying is finally the likeness of Christ, the one in whom God is seen.

1.reflection:
The elder’s greatest joy is to hear that his children are walking in the truth (v. 4). What does walking in the truth look like in ordinary life? Whom would you most love to hear it about, and who might be glad to hear it about you?

Gaius cared for strangers simply because they belonged to Christ and had gone out for his name (vv. 5–8). What would it look like for your household and your church to be “fellow workers for the truth” with those who carry the gospel today?

Diotrephes is not accused of false doctrine, yet he “likes to put himself first” (v. 9). Where does the love of being first show itself in churches, and in you? How does Jesus answer it in Mark 10:42–45?

Demetrius “has received a good testimony from everyone, and from the truth itself” (v. 12). Whom do you know like that, and what would it take for your own life to bear that kind of testimony?
